**ORIGINAL PAPER**

# Early Childhood Maltreatment and Adolescent Aggressive Behaviors: A Causal Mediation Analysis of Callous-Unemotional Traits

### Callous Traits Mediate Child Abuse and Aggression

**Dongxue Zhu1,2 · Chuchu Li1 · Fan Wang1 · Yonghan Li1 · Mengyuan Yuan1 · Yuan Li1 · Leilei Cao1 · Shaojie Wang1 · Gengfu Wang1,3,4 · Puyu Su1,3,4** [** ·**](http://orcid.org/0000-0002-0946-2805) **Yuqi Kang5**

Received: 28 April 2024 / Accepted: 19 December 2025 / Published online: 6 January 2026 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2025

**Abstract** Child maltreatment (CM) and callous-unemotional (CU) traits have been linked to aggressive behaviors in adolescence; however, the underlying pathways and causal nature of these links require further investigation. The present study exam- ined how CM influenced aggressive behaviors, accounting for subtype distinctions and gender-specific patterns. This study is based on longitudinal data from 1,592 students from the Chinese Early Adolescent Cohort in Anhui Province. Information on early CM prior to seventh grade was obtained at baseline; CU traits and aggressive behaviors were col- lected during follow-up. Participants were required to complete self-report questionnaires. Causal mediation analysis was conducted in RStudio 3.4.0, with adjustment for baseline confounders to clarify pathways between CM and aggression. Linear regression results showed that emotional abuse (_b_ = 0.94, 95% CI: 0.53–1.35, _P_ \< 0.05), physical abuse (_b_ = 1.14, 95% CI: 0.48–1.81, _P_ \< 0.05), and emotional neglect (_b_ = 1.17, 95% CI: 0.64–1.70, _P_ \< 0.05) were significantly associated with adolescents’ aggressive behaviors. Mediation analyses indicated that CU traits accounted for 15% of the overall CM effect, with stronger mediation observed in boys (21%) across subtypes, but not in girls. These results support the importance of focusing on enhancing healthy personality development and reducing emotional detachment, and foster- ing emotional connection when working psychotherapeutically with adolescents who have experienced CM. In addition, reducing CM incidence and promoting healthier personality trajectories represent essential strategies for mitigating aggres- sive behaviors in adolescence.

## Highlights

- Multiple types of child maltreatment may occur simultaneously.
- Child maltreatment subtype and gender impact adolescent aggressive behaviors.
- Emotional abuse and emotional neglect are related to aggressive behaviors in girls.
- The mediating effect of callous-unemotional traits was observed only in boys.

**Keywords** Early adolescents · Child maltreatment · Callous-unemotional traits · Aggressive behaviors · Mediating effects

Dongxue Zhu and Chuchu Li contributed equally to this work.

## Discussion

This study aims to examine how different dimensions of CM (types, cumulative exposure, and gender) influence adoles- cent aggressive behaviors, and to investigate the mediating role of CU traits in this association, with a particular focus on gender differences in the mediating pathways. This lon- gitudinal investigation demonstrated that the impact of CM on aggressive behaviors differed according to type, cumula- tive exposure, and gender. CU traits functioned as media- tors of the CM–aggression pathway exclusively among boys, highlighting gender-specific mechanisms underlying this association. The results provide a basis for advancing research on causal mediation linking CM, CU traits, and aggressive behaviors.

### Childhood Maltreatment and Aggressive Behaviors

A significant association between CM and aggressive behaviors emerged in this study. Consistent with the Cycle of Violence Theory, individuals exposed to CM are predis- posed to aggressive behavior later in life (Xiao et al., [2023)](#authors-and-affiliations). Emotional numbing and difficulties in processing fear- related emotions may contribute to the use of aggression as a form of release (Kim-Spoon et al., 2013). Furthermore, experiences of CM often engender feelings of rejection and 

devaluation, reducing self-esteem and increasing the likeli- hood of aggression (Glaser, 2002).

Research has demonstrated that all categories of CM predict heightened risk of violent aggression during ado- lescence and adulthood (Xiao et al., [2020)](#authors-and-affiliations). In contrast, the present study identified significant associations only with 

cies (Wang et al., [2020a,](#authors-and-affiliations) [b;](#authors-and-affiliations) Wolf & Elklit, [2020;](#authors-and-affiliations) Xiang et al., [2020)](#authors-and-affiliations).

Moreover, aggression severity rose with the accumula- tion of maltreatment types. This observation is consistent with prior evidence of high co-occurrence across CM forms, with up to 69% of adolescents exposed to multiple maltreat- ment experiences (Finkelhor et al., 2007). Adolescents sub- jected to polyvictimization display greater psychological trauma and emotional distress, accompanied by an elevated likelihood of engaging in aggressive behaviors (Mitchell et al., 2020).

### Mediating Role of Callous-Unemotional Traits

Analysis indicated that CU traits served as a mediator between CM and aggressive behavior, explaining approxi- mately 15% of the overall association. CM contributes to the development of CU traits, which subsequently heighten the likelihood of aggressive responses, consistent with the patterns observed in cross-sectional research (Li et al., 2022). Unlike cross-sectional evidence, however, the pres- ent investigation offers more reliable support for causal inference. Neuroimaging studies have further identified functional impairments in emotion-related brain regions, including the amygdala and medial ventral prefrontal cor- tex, among individuals exhibiting CU traits (Finger et al., 2008). Such individuals frequently display diminished sen- sitivity to the consequences of their actions for others and often interpret aggression as an acceptable strategy for con- flict resolution (Kimonis et al., 2004). Heightened anger in response to stressors may foster maladaptive coping tenden- cies, which are expressed through aggressive conduct (Carl- son et al., [2015;](#confined-to-boys-exposed-to-emotional-abuse-and-neglect-o-h-e-a-l-t-h--2-0-1-7--0-2--0-0-2-these-results-offer-relevant-insights-for-policy-development-baumrind-d-1991-the-influence-of-parenting-style-on-adolescent-and-clinical-practice-competence-and-substance-use-the-journal-of-early-adoles-) Del Giudice et al., 2011).
